## PDF page 114

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=114)

```text
                      FACING RAISES


You can also face raises that offer you incorrect pot odds. But before you
muck your hand, you should still calculate your implied odds first.

The formula and methodology are the same for calculating implied odds
whether you are facing bets or raises. You can either use the formula or
compare ratios. The key thing to remember is that once you bet, that bet
belongs to the pot and no longer to you.

For example, if the pot is $500 before you bet $200 into it and you face a raise
to $750 total, you would be calling $550 to win $1,450. This gives you 2.6:1 pot
odds.

If you assume that you have 20% equity, which requires 4:1 pot odds, the gap
between 4 and 2.6 is 1.4. Multiply 1.4 by how much you need to call ($550), and
you can eyeball the minimum amount of extra money you need to make on
future streets.

Each page contains two examples. Read the prompt to find the estimated
equity of your hand, the original pot size, and the size of your bet. Then com-
plete the table below for the three possible total raise sizes. E.g., if you bet
$150 into $200, their raise size of $400 means you need to call $250 more.

GLGL.




                                   PA G E 1 1 4
```

## PDF page 118

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=118)

```text
                                 CHAPTER EIGHT



          BREAKEVEN PERCENTAGE


Breakeven percentage (BE%) is the mathematical way of stating when a bet
or raise is outright 0EV. If your opponent folds more often than the breakeven
%, you make an auto-profit. If they fold less often than the breakeven %, your
bluff would take an immediate loss.

That is not to say that all bluffs need to be auto-profitable though. A bluff
that fails to be auto-profitable on an earlier street can still be part of a +EV
line when factoring in future streets, playability, and edges.

But more on all of that later.

For now, you need to know the formula for this:

                         B E % = R I S K / ( R I S K + R E WA R D)


Where the risk is the size of your bet or raise, and the reward is the size of the
pot you are fighting for. Simply put, the bigger your bet compared to the pot
size, the more often your bluff needs to work. The smaller your bet, the less
often your bluff needs to work.

These exercises will guide you through some simple examples to practice
calculating your BE% when you are making bets.




                                       PA G E 1 1 8
```

```text
                     B R E A K E V E N P E R C E N TAG E: B E T T I N G


TOOLS TO USE: Seasoned players should be able to do this off the top of
their heads. If you are just starting out with BE% you can download & use my
“Breakeven Percentage” spreadsheet at www.splitsuit.pro/sheets

PROCESS: Each page contains two exercises where you are given the pot size
before you bet and five possible bet sizes that you could make. Complete the
table below, jotting down what percentage of the pot each of the bet sizes
represents, and the BE% for each.




TAKEAWAYS: The BE% is directly related to the size of your bet compared to
the size of the pot. A $0.25 bet into a $0.50 pot has the same BE% as betting
$440K into a pot of $880K.

Memorize the BE% for common bet sizes like half-pot, 2/3rd pot, and full pot.

GLGL.




                                        PA G E 1 1 9
```
